issues.legal_issue: Property inherited by a sole holder that becomes Mitakshara coparcenary property on the birth of a son is governed, on the holder’s later death, by the rules for devolution of coparcenary interest rather than the general rules for separate property.
material_facts: The property had been inherited by a member of a Mitakshara family when he had no son, so it was then his separate property.
A son was born to him before the Hindu Succession Act came into force, and the property thereafter became coparcenary property under Mitakshara law.
The holder died intestate leaving sons and daughters, including female heirs specified in Class I of the Schedule.
issues.conclusion: The property was coparcenary property when the holder died. His coparcenary interest was governed by Section 6, and because he left female Class I heirs, that interest devolved by intestate succession rather than survivorship. Section 8 did not govern that coparcenary interest; the holder’s half share devolved upon his heirs and legal representatives.
issues.legal_principle: Under Mitakshara law, property inherited by a person from a paternal ancestor may remain separate while he has no son, but becomes coparcenary property as against a son when one is born. Krishna Prasad v. C.I.T., Bangalore, and the authorities discussed in Pratap Narain v. Commissioner of Income-Tax, U.P., support the property’s ancestral or coparcenary character. Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act governs a deceased coparcener’s interest, and its proviso requires intestate or testamentary succession rather than survivorship when a Class I female relative survives. Section 8 governs property devolving as separate property; under Chander Sen, property inherited under Section 8 is taken individually, not as karta of the heir’s own family. Eramma v. Veerupana and Daya Singh v. Dhan Kaur establish that the Act is not retrospective and does not apply where succession opened before it came into force. Section 4 gives the Act overriding effect over inconsistent prior Hindu law. The 2005 amendment did not apply because succession had already opened before that amendment.

rule.if: succession_appeal and inherited_property and son_born_before_succession_reform and female_class_one_heir_survived

predicates.succession_appeal: The dispute is an appeal concerning how a deceased person’s property devolves among heirs.
predicates.inherited_property: The holder received the property by inheritance from an ancestor.
predicates.son_born_before_succession_reform: A son was born to the holder before the applicable succession-law change, causing the inherited property to be treated as coparcenary property as against him.
predicates.female_class_one_heir_survived: A female heir in the first class of heirs survived the holder.

issues.definition: When an inheritance dispute involves property that became coparcenary property on the birth of a son and a female first-class heir survived, the deceased holder’s coparcenary interest devolves by succession rather than survivorship.

issues.legal_issue: A son’s entitlement to claim coparcenary status based on birth before a succession-law change must be supported by evidence of that birth.
material_facts: One son was born before the Hindu Succession Act came into force and was a coparcener.
The record contained no evidence that the other son was born before the Act came into force.
The deceased left both sons and daughters as heirs.
issues.conclusion: The other son could not be shown to derive a coparcenary entitlement on the basis that he was born before the Act came into force. He nevertheless remained among the heirs entitled to share in the deceased’s interest that devolved by intestate succession.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act to the deceased coparcener’s interest and required a factual basis for treating a son as having acquired coparcenary status by birth before the Act came into force. The Court noted that no evidence established the relevant birth fact for the other son; it did not exclude him from inheriting the deceased’s interest as an heir. The distinction between coparcenary property and property inherited individually under Section 8 is explained in Chander Sen and the authorities following it, including Commissioner of Income Tax v. P.L. Karuppan Chettiar and Additional Commissioner of Income Tax v. M. Karthikeyan.

predicates.succession_appeal: The dispute is an appeal concerning the devolution of a deceased person’s property among heirs.
predicates.son_claims_coparcenary_status_by_birth: A son’s claimed coparcenary entitlement depends on his having acquired an interest by birth before a succession-law change.
predicates.no_evidence_of_pre_reform_birth: The record contains no evidence that the son was born before that change.

issues.definition: When a son’s claimed coparcenary status depends on birth before a succession-law change and the record does not establish that birth, his coparcenary entitlement is not established, though his heirship remains.
